hints: Think about which two subshells lose electrons when a transition metal ionises, and how much energy difference there is between removing an electron from each one.
walkthrough:
Picture where the electrons live**
Iron is $[Ar] 3d^6 4s^2$. When it forms ions, electrons come first from $4s$ then from $3d$. The key point is that these two subshells sit almost at the same energy level, unlike, say, $2p$ and $3s$ in a main group element where there is a big jump.

Link similar energy to variable loss**
Because $3d$ and $4s$ are so close in energy, it costs only a little extra energy to remove one more $d$ electron. So $Fe$ can lose just the two $4s$ electrons to give $Fe^{2+}$, or two $4s$ plus one $3d$ to give $Fe^{3+}$, both with stable arrangements. That is why many different oxidation states are accessible.
Final answer: The $(3)d$ and $(4)s$ subshells are very close / similar in energy, so variable numbers of electrons can be removed using similar amounts of energy.

hints: Break the term apart: what is at the centre of the species, and what species are attached around it by coordinate bonds?
walkthrough:
Build the definition in two halves**
Always start at the centre. A complex has a central transition metal atom or ion, here $Fe^{2+}$ in $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$. Then look around it. It is surrounded by molecules or ions called ligands, here six $H_2O$ molecules, each donating a lone pair to form a coordinate bond to the metal. Put those two ideas together and you have the full definition.
Final answer: A species / ion formed by a central metal atom / ion surrounded by / bonded to one or more ligands.

hints: Compare the ligands on each side: $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ changes to $[Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2]$. Where could $OH^-$ come from, and what physical change do you see when this happens?
walkthrough:
Spot the ligand change**
On the left you have six $H_2O$ ligands. On the right two of them have become $OH^-$ ligands to give neutral $[Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2]$. That tells you $OH^-$ ions must have been added, most simply as dilute $NaOH(aq)$ or $NH_3(aq)$ as a source of $OH^-$.

Name the reaction type correctly**
Two $H_2O$ ligands are deprotonated by $OH^-$ acting as a base: $[Fe(H_2O)_6]^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow [Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2] + 2H_2O$. Because a neutral solid comes out of solution, Cambridge also accepts precipitation, and because $OH^-$ replaces part of the $H_2O$ sphere it can be called ligand exchange.

Final answer: reagent: $NaOH(aq)$ / $OH^-(aq)$
type of reaction: precipitation / ligand exchange / acid-base / deprotonation

hints: The green $Fe(II)$ precipitate turns to brown $Fe(III)$ $[Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3]$. Think about what in air could cause oxidation and which half equation in Table 2.1 involves the iron species.

Recall how to decide if oxidation by $O_2$ is feasible: compare the $E^\circ$ of the $O_2 / OH^-$ couple with the $E^\circ$ of the iron couple, or calculate $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode}$.

To write the overall equation, multiply the iron reduction equation to balance electrons with the $O_2$ equation, then reverse the iron equation because iron is being oxidised, and cancel $e^-$, $H_2O$ and $OH^-$ as needed.
walkthrough:
Identify oxidation and the oxidant**
Green $[Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2]$ contains $Fe(II)$. Brown $[Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3]$ contains $Fe(III)$. So iron has increased in oxidation number from +2 to +3, it has been oxidised. The only oxidant available on standing in air is oxygen, $O_2$ dissolved from the air.

Prove it with electrode potentials**
Look at Table 2.1. The iron couple $Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3 + H_2O + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2 + OH^-$ has $E^\circ = -0.56\, V$. The oxygen couple $O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightleftharpoons 4OH^-$ has $E^\circ = +0.40\, V$. Oxygen has the more positive $E^\circ$, so it will be reduced while the $Fe(II)$ species is oxidised. The cell emf is: $$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = +0.40 - (-0.56) = +0.96\, V$$ A positive value confirms the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

Combine the half equations**
Reverse the iron equation for oxidation and multiply by 4 to supply 4 electrons for $O_2$: $$4Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2 + 4OH^- \rightarrow 4Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3 + 4H_2O + 4e^-$$ $$O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-$$ Add and cancel $4e^-$, $4OH^-$ and part of the $H_2O$ to leave: $$4Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 4Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3 + 2H_2O$$ That brown product is $Fe(III)$ hydroxide, often written simply as $Fe(OH)_3$.

Final answer: $[Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2]$ is oxidised from +2 to +3 on standing in air by $O_2$.
$E^\circ_{cell} = (+0.40) - (-0.56) = +0.96\, V$, positive so reaction is feasible / $E^\circ$ for $O_2$ is more positive than $E^\circ$ for the Fe couple.
$4Fe(H_2O)_4(OH)_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 4Fe(H_2O)_3(OH)_3 + 2H_2O$

hints: Recall the link between free energy and cell potential: $\Delta G^\ominus = -nE^\circ_{cell}F$. Focus on finding $n$, the total moles of electrons transferred in reaction 1 as written.
Check the change in oxidation number: each $Co^{2+}$ to $Co^{3+}$ is one electron, and the equation shows two cobalt complexes reacting. Use $F = 96500\, C\, mol^{-1}$ and convert J to kJ.
walkthrough:
Find n from the stoichiometry**
Reaction 1 is $2[Co(NH_3)_6]^{2+} + H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+} + 2OH^-$. Each $Co(II)$ to $Co(III)$ loses one electron, and there are two cobalt ions, so total electrons transferred $n = 2$. This is also the electrons gained by $H_2O_2$.

Substitute into Delta G expression**
Use $$\Delta G^\ominus = -nE^\circ_{cell}F$$ with $E^\circ_{cell} = +1.67\, V$ and $F = 96500\, C\, mol^{-1}$: $$\Delta G^\ominus = -2 \times 1.67 \times 96500$$ $$ = -322270\, J\, mol^{-1}$$ Divide by 1000 for kJ: $$\Delta G^\ominus = -322.3\, kJ\, mol^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the oxidation is feasible, as expected from the large positive $E^\circ_{cell}$.

Final answer: $\Delta G^\ominus = -nE^\circ_{cell}F$ with $n = 2$
$\Delta G^\ominus = -2 \times 1.67 \times 96500 = -322270\, J\, mol^{-1} = -322.3\, kJ\, mol^{-1}$
